title: Book 23 — Penelope eventually recognises her husband—early in the morning Odysseus, Telemachus, Eumaeus, and Philoetius leave the town
paragraphs: Euryclea went upstairs laughing to tell her mistress that her dear husband had come home. Her old knees felt young again and her feet were quick with joy as she climbed to her mistress and bent over her head to speak. "Wake up, Penelope, my dear child," she cried, "and see with your own eyes something you've been waiting for all this time. Odysseus has truly come home at last, and he's killed the suitors who were causing so much trouble in his house, eating up his estate and mistreating his son."

"My good nurse," Penelope replied, "you must be losing your mind. The gods sometimes drive sensible people mad, and make foolish people wise. This is what they must have done to you—you were always such a reasonable person before. Why are you mocking me when I already have enough troubles, talking such nonsense and waking me from the sweet sleep that had finally closed my eyes? I haven't slept so soundly since the day my poor husband left for that cursed city. Go back to the women's quarters. If anyone else had woken me with such ridiculous news, I would have sent her away with a harsh scolding. Only your age protects you now."

"My dear child," Euryclea answered, "I'm not mocking you. It's completely true—Odysseus has come home again. He was the stranger they all kept treating so badly in the courtyard. Telemachus knew the whole time that his father had returned, but kept the secret so they could take revenge on all those wicked men."

Then Penelope sprang up from her bed, threw her arms around Euryclea, and wept with joy. "But my dear nurse," she said, "explain this to me. If he's really come home as you say, how did he manage to overcome all those wicked suitors by himself, considering how many there were?"

"I wasn't there," Euryclea answered, "and don't know the details. I only heard them groaning as they died. We sat huddled together in a corner of the women's room with the doors shut, until your son came to get me because his father sent him. Then I found Odysseus standing over the corpses lying all around him on the ground, one on top of another. You would have been thrilled to see him standing there covered in blood and dirt, looking just like a lion. But the bodies are now piled up in the gatehouse in the outer court, and Odysseus has lit a great fire to purify the house with sulfur. He sent me to call you, so come with me so you can both be happy together at last. Now your heart's desire has been fulfilled—your husband has come home to find both wife and son alive and well, and to take his revenge in his own house on the suitors who treated him so badly."

"My dear nurse," said Penelope, "don't celebrate too confidently over all this. You know how delighted everyone would be to see Odysseus come home—especially myself and the son born to both of us. But what you're telling me can't possibly be true. It must be some god who was angry with the suitors for their great wickedness and destroyed them. They respected no one in the whole world, neither rich nor poor, who came near them, and they've met a bad end because of their crimes. Odysseus is dead far from Greek lands—he will never return home again."

Then nurse Euryclea said, "My child, what are you saying? You've always been so stubborn and convinced that your husband would never return, even though he's in the house right now by his own fireside. Besides, I can give you another proof. When I was washing him, I saw the scar the wild boar gave him, and I wanted to tell you about it, but he wisely wouldn't let me and covered my mouth with his hands. So come with me, and I'll make this deal with you—if I'm lying to you, you can have me killed in the cruelest way you can imagine."

"My dear nurse," said Penelope, "however wise you may be, you can hardly understand the plans of the gods. Nevertheless, we'll go find my son, so I can see the corpses of the suitors and the man who killed them."

With that, she came down from her upper room, wondering whether she should keep her distance from her husband and question him, or go straight to him and embrace him. When she had crossed the stone floor of the courtyard, she sat down across from Odysseus by the fire, against the wall, while Odysseus sat near one of the pillars, looking at the ground and waiting to see what his wise wife would say when she saw him. For a long time she sat silent, as if stunned. One moment she looked him full in the face, but then again she was misled by his shabby clothes and failed to recognize him, until Telemachus began to scold her and said:

"Mother—though you're so hard-hearted I can barely call you that—why do you stay away from my father like this? Why don't you sit beside him and start talking to him and asking questions? No other woman could bear to keep away from her husband when he'd returned to her after twenty years away, after going through so much. But your heart was always as hard as stone."

Penelope answered, "My son, I'm so amazed I can't find words to ask questions or answer them. I can't even look him straight in the face. Still, if he really is Odysseus come back to his own home, we'll get to know each other better soon enough, for there are signs that only the two of us know, hidden from everyone else."

Odysseus smiled at this and said to Telemachus, "Let your mother test me however she wants. She'll make up her mind soon enough. Right now she rejects me and thinks I'm someone else because I'm covered with dirt and wearing such poor clothes. But let's think about what we should do next. When someone kills another man—even one who wouldn't leave many friends to avenge him—the killer must still say goodbye to his friends and flee the country. But we've been killing the pillars of a whole town, all the finest young men of Ithaca. Think about this carefully."

"Look to it yourself, father," Telemachus answered, "for they say you're the wisest counselor in the world, and no other mortal can compare with you. We'll follow you gladly, and you won't find us failing you as long as our strength holds out."

"I'll tell you what I think is best," Odysseus replied. "First, wash and put on clean clothes. Tell the maids to go to their rooms and dress properly too. Then Phemius will play a lively dance tune on his lyre, so that if people outside hear it, or any neighbors, or someone passing in the street notices, they'll think there's a wedding in the house, and no rumors about the suitors' deaths will spread through town before we can escape to the woods on my land. Once there, we'll decide which course heaven offers us seems wisest."

He spoke, and they did exactly as he said. First they washed and put on clean shirts, while the women got ready. Then Phemius took his lyre and filled them all with longing for sweet song and stately dance. The house echoed with the sound of men and women dancing, and people outside said, "I suppose the queen has finally gotten married. She should be ashamed of herself for not continuing to protect her husband's property until he comes home."

That's what they said, but they didn't know what had really happened. The head servant Eurynome washed and anointed Odysseus in his own house and gave him a shirt and cloak, while Athena made him look taller and stronger than before. She also made thick hair grow on his head and flow down in curls like hyacinth blossoms. She made him glorious about the head and shoulders, just as a skilled craftsman who has learned his art from Hephaestus and Athena—whose work is full of beauty—enhances a piece of silver by gilding it. He came from the bath looking like one of the immortals and sat down across from his wife in the chair he had left. "My dear," he said, "heaven has given you a heart more stubborn than any woman ever had. No other woman could bear to stay away from her husband when he'd returned to her after twenty years away, after going through so much. Come, nurse, prepare a bed for me. I'll sleep alone, since this woman has a heart as hard as iron."

"My dear," Penelope answered, "I don't want to seem proud or to put you down, but I'm not impressed by your appearance, for I remember very well what kind of man you were when you sailed from Ithaca. Nevertheless, Euryclea, take his bed outside the bedroom that he built himself. Bring the bed out of that room and put bedding on it with fleeces, good covers, and blankets."

She said this to test him, but Odysseus grew angry and said, "Wife, I'm very upset by what you just said. Who has been moving my bed from where I left it? It would be a hard task for even the most skilled craftsman, unless some god came to help him move it. No living man, however strong and in his prime, could shift it from its place, for it's a marvelous creation that I made with my own hands. There was a young olive tree growing within the grounds of the house, full of vigor and about as thick as a pillar. I built my room around this tree with strong stone walls and a roof to cover them, and made the doors strong and well-fitted. Then I cut off the top branches of the olive tree and left the trunk standing. I shaped this roughly from the root up, then worked it carefully with tools, making it straight by drawing a line on the wood, and turned it into a bedpost. I bored a hole down the middle and made it the center post of my bed, working on it until I finished it, inlaying it with gold and silver. After this I stretched a hide of crimson leather from one side to the other. So you see I know all about it, and I want to learn whether it's still there, or whether someone has moved it by cutting down the olive tree at its roots."

When she heard the clear proof Odysseus gave her, she broke down completely. She ran weeping to his side, threw her arms around his neck, and kissed him. "Don't be angry with me, Odysseus," she cried, "you who are the wisest of all mankind. We have both suffered. Heaven has denied us the happiness of spending our youth and growing old together. So don't be upset or offended that I didn't embrace you as soon as I saw you. I've been trembling with fear the whole time that someone might come here and deceive me with a lying story, for there are many wicked people around. Helen, Zeus's daughter, would never have given herself to a foreign man if she had known that the Greeks would come after her and bring her back. Heaven put it in her heart to do wrong, and she gave no thought to that sin which has been the source of all our sorrows. But now that you've convinced me by showing you know all about our bed—which no human being has ever seen except you and me and one maid, Actor's daughter, whom my father gave me when I married and who guards our bedroom door—stubborn as I've been, I can doubt no longer."

Then Odysseus melted in turn and wept as he held his dear and faithful wife. As the sight of land is welcome to swimmers making for shore when Poseidon has wrecked their ship with furious winds and waves—a few reach land alone, covered with brine, and are thankful to find themselves on solid ground and out of danger—just so welcome was her husband to her as she looked at him, and she couldn't take her arms from around his neck. Indeed, they would have gone on sharing their joy until rosy-fingered Dawn appeared, if Athena hadn't decided otherwise and held night back in the far west, while not allowing Dawn to leave Ocean or harness her two horses Lampus and Phaethon that bring daylight to mankind.

At last, however, Odysseus said, "Wife, we haven't reached the end of our troubles yet. I still have an unknown amount of difficult work to do. It's long and hard, but I must go through with it, for this is what the ghost of Tiresias prophesied about me when I went down to Hades to ask about my return and that of my companions. But now let's go to bed, so we can lie down and enjoy the blessed gift of sleep."

"You can go to bed whenever you like," Penelope replied, "now that the gods have brought you home to your own house and country. But since heaven has put it in your mind to speak of it, tell me about the task ahead of you. I'll have to hear about it eventually, so it's better I know now."

"My dear," Odysseus answered, "why do you insist I tell you? Still, I won't hide it from you, though you won't like it. I don't like it myself, for Tiresias told me to travel far and wide, carrying an oar, until I came to a country where people have never heard of the sea and don't even use salt in their food. They know nothing about ships or oars that are like a ship's wings. He gave me this sure sign, which I won't hide from you: he said a traveler would meet me and ask if the thing on my shoulder was a winnowing fan. When that happens, I must plant my oar in the ground and sacrifice a ram, bull, and boar to Poseidon. After that I should go home and offer sacrifices to all the gods in heaven, one after another. As for myself, he said death would come to me from the sea, and my life would ebb away very gently when I'm full of years and peace, and my people would bless me. All this, he said, would surely come to pass."
And Penelope said, "If the gods are going to give you a happier time in your old age, you can hope then to have some relief from misfortune."

That's how they talked. Meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse brought torches and prepared the bed with soft covers. As soon as they had arranged everything, the nurse went back into the house to rest, leaving Eurynome, the bedroom attendant, to lead Odysseus and Penelope to bed by torchlight. When she had shown them to their room, she left, and they came joyfully to their own old bed. Telemachus, Philoetius, and the swineherd stopped dancing and made the women stop too. Then they lay down to sleep in the courtyard.

When Odysseus and Penelope had satisfied their love, they lay talking together. She told him how much she had endured, seeing the house filled with a crowd of wicked suitors who had killed so many sheep and cattle on her account and drunk so many jars of wine. Odysseus in turn told her what he had suffered and how much trouble he had caused others. He told her everything, and she was so delighted to listen that she never fell asleep until he had finished his whole story.

He began with his victory over the Cicones, and how he then reached the fertile land of the Lotus-eaters. He told her all about the Cyclops and how he had punished him for so ruthlessly eating his brave companions. How he went on to Aeolus, who received him hospitably and helped him on his way, but even so he couldn't reach home, for to his great grief a storm carried him out to sea again. How he came to the Laestrygonian city of Telepylus, where the people destroyed all his ships and crews except himself and his own ship. Then he told of cunning Circe and her magic, and how he sailed to the cold house of Hades to consult the ghost of the Theban prophet Tiresias, and saw his old comrades and his mother who bore and raised him as a child. How he heard the wonderful singing of the Sirens, and went on to the Wandering Rocks and terrible Charybdis and Scylla, whom no man had ever passed safely. How his men then ate the cattle of the sun god, and Zeus therefore struck their ship with thunderbolts, so all his men died together while he alone survived. How at last he reached the island of Ogygia and the nymph Calypso, who kept him in a cave and fed him, wanting him to marry her and make him immortal so he would never grow old, but she couldn't persuade him to agree. And how after much suffering he found his way to the Phaeacians, who treated him like a god and sent him back to his own country in a ship, after giving him gold, bronze, and clothing in great abundance. This was the last thing he told her about, for here deep sleep took hold of him and eased the burden of his sorrows.

Then Athena thought of another matter. When she decided Odysseus had had enough of his wife and rest, she told golden-throned Dawn to rise from Ocean and shed light on mankind. At this, Odysseus rose from his comfortable bed and said to Penelope, "Wife, we've both had our full share of troubles—you here, lamenting my absence, and I being prevented from getting home though I longed to all the time. Now that we've finally come together, take care of the property in the house. As for the sheep and goats the wicked suitors ate, I'll take many myself by force from other people, and make the Greeks replace the rest until they've filled all my pens. I'm going now to the wooded countryside to see my father, who has grieved so long on my account. And to you I give these instructions, though you hardly need them: at sunrise word will spread immediately that I've been killing the suitors. Go upstairs and stay there with your women. See no one and ask no questions."

As he spoke, he put on his armor. Then he woke Telemachus, Philoetius, and Eumaeus, and told them all to arm themselves too. They did so and put on their weapons. When they were ready, they opened the gates and went out, with Odysseus leading the way. It was now daylight, but Athena still concealed them in darkness and led them quickly out of the town.
